column4: Salih assigns the she-camel a drink and the people a known day's drink (شِرْبٌ مَعْلُومٌ); this makes the violated water share in the section concrete and apportioned.
The messenger explicitly forbids harming the camel and warns of punishment; the ayah supplies the boundary the people choose to cross.
The people hamstring the camel (فَعَقَرُوهَا) and regret it; this is the act and immediate human response behind the section's account of a transgression.
Its contribution is the punishment that follows their camel-killing, completing the prior ayah's image of regret with the consequence.
God says He is sending the she-camel as a trial (فِتْنَةً لَهُمْ), matching the section's camel as a divine sending and test of restraint.
The water is divided between them (الْمَاءُ قِسْمَةٌ بَيْنَهُمْ), giving the section's camel and people distinct measured shares.
They call their companion, who then hamstrings the camel (فَنَادَوْا صَاحِبَهُمْ ... فَعَقَرَ); the act is initiated by the people, as the section says the rebel sends himself into action.
The question about the punishment and warnings follows the hamstringing, so this ayah contributes the announced consequence to the water-share scene.

One blast turns them into dry fragments like a fence-maker's brushwood (كَأَنَّهُمْ هَشِيمُ الْمُحْتَظِرِ); it connects the people's ruin with the section's field made barren and structures flattened.
Salih calls the she-camel God's sign and orders them to leave her grazing and not harm her; it gives the camel's divine ownership and protected share explicit form.
Thamud are settled in the land and take palaces from its plains (سُهُولِهَا قُصُورًا), directly grounding the section's plain, palaces, and their later leveling.
The people hamstring the camel and defy their Lord's command (فَعَقَرُوا النَّاقَةَ وَعَتَوْا); this is the section's violation of the sign and its limit.
The earthquake leaves them prostrate in their homes; this ayah supplies the bodily and domestic aftermath of the prior camel-killing.
Salih names the she-camel as God's sign, gives her grazing ground, and prohibits harm; it states the protected animal and boundary at the heart of the section.
After they hamstring her, Salih gives them three days before the promise is fulfilled; the ayah makes the consequence follow the act in time.
Salih and the believers who were with him are saved by mercy as the punishment arrives; this gives the section's two moral fields distinct outcomes.
The cry seizes the wrongdoers in their homes, completing the earlier warning with the consequence that falls on the people who killed the camel.
Their homes seem never to have been inhabited; the emptied settlement makes the section's leveled plain and vanished houses perceptible.
God calls camels among His rites and commands His name over them at sacrifice; this contrasts an authorized, grateful offering with Thamud's forbidden destruction of God's sign.
The ayah says neither camel flesh nor blood reaches God, but piety does (وَلَٰكِنْ يَنَالُهُ التَّقْوَىٰ مِنْكُمْ); it makes the section's restraint behind bodily acts explicit.
The verse names Thamud's houses fallen in ruin because of their wrongdoing (فَتِلْكَ بُيُوتُهُمْ خَاوِيَةً بِمَا ظَلَمُوا); it directly joins their guilt to the collapse of their built place.
Those who believed and were mindful are saved; this adjacent outcome completes the ruin of Thamud with the contrasting field of protection.

Thamud are shown the way but choose blindness over guidance, then the humiliating thunderbolt seizes them; this states the section's wrong choice and its consequence in another account of the same people.
God does not destroy a town before sending a messenger to recite His signs; this states the divine order of messenger-before-judgment that the section sees in Salih's mission to Thamud.
The verse says God sent (بَعَثَ) a messenger among the believers; that same sending action clarifies the section's contrast between God's sent messenger and the man who raises himself.
Water bursts from the rock into springs (فَانْفَجَرَتْ مِنْهُ اثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ عَيْنًا); this is the water-gushing branch of the section's f-j-r meeting.
The earth is made to burst into springs (وَفَجَّرْنَا الْأَرْضَ عُيُونًا) as floodwater meets the rain; it supplies the section's image of a burst that overflows its bounds.
The sky's gates open with pouring water (بِمَاءٍ مُنْهَمِرٍ); this preceding ayah supplies the flood's rain source before the next verse's earth springs.
The oath is by dawn (وَالْفَجْرِ), the same named word-family the section connects to fujūr's image of a split opening in the night.
Dawn is described as breathing (وَالصُّبْحِ إِذَا تَنَفَّسَ) after the night recedes in 81:17; this gives a close image of night giving way to opening light.
The night is sworn by as it recedes (وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا عَسْعَسَ); the next dawn verse completes the section's night-to-opening transition.
The fast ends at dawn, distinguished from night by the white thread of daybreak; the boundary between covering night and opened day is explicit here.
The verse names “the garment of God-consciousness” (وَلِبَاسُ التَّقْوَىٰ), directly matching the section's secondary image of taqwa as a protective covering.
Joseph's speaker says the soul persistently urges evil (إِنَّ النَّفْسَ لَأَمَّارَةٌ بِالسُّوءِ); this gives the section's inward fujūr a direct formulation.
God raises heaven's ceiling and proportions it (فَسَوَّاهَا), repeating the sawwā of the section's formed sky and setting up its contrast with Thamud's leveling.
The passage asks whether creating heaven or people is harder, then says God built it; this begins the same heaven-to-earth construction sequence that echoes the section's created order.
This next ayah darkens heaven's night and brings out its morning; it supplies the ordered covering and opening that follows the fashioned sky.
The earth is spread out (دَحَاهَا), a direct parallel in image to the section's spread ground between sky and soul and its plain made level.
The following verse brings water and pasture out of the earth; it makes the fertile ground in the section dependent on provision from above.
Pasture is made provision for people and their cattle (مَتَاعًا لَكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ), completing the prior water-and-ground scene with its herds.
The verse describes night as a sign from which daylight is stripped away; this is a close reverse view of the section's day opening and night covering.
The sun runs to its appointed course; its assigned motion supports the section's opening picture of each body keeping its place.
The moon is assigned its phases; this contributes the ordered lunar following that the section sets beside the sun and day.
Neither sun overtakes the moon nor night outstrips day, each moving in an orbit (كُلٌّ فِي فَلَكٍ يَسْبَحُونَ); this states the ordered alternation at the beginning of the section.
God wraps night over day and day over night (يُكَوِّرُ اللَّيْلَ عَلَى النَّهَارِ); this is the ordered covering and uncovering against which the section sets the soul's breach of restraint.
Night and day are made to succeed one another (خِلْفَةً) for remembrance and gratitude; this directly connects the section's closing turn of night and day with recurring succession.
The verse repeats the night-covering formula (وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَىٰ), directly echoing the section's night that covers in its appointed turn.
Day is sworn by as it appears (وَالنَّهَارِ إِذَا تَجَلَّىٰ); this gives the opening of light that complements the preceding covering night.
God pours water abundantly (أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا الْمَاءَ صَبًّا); this begins the rain-to-field sequence behind the section's fertile plain.
The earth is split open (ثُمَّ شَقَقْنَا الْأَرْضَ شَقًّا), followed by crops; the ayah gives the broken soil from which a living field emerges.
Grain is brought forth from that split earth (فَأَنْبَتْنَا فِيهَا حَبًّا); it supplies the crop-growth side of the section's contrast with barren ground.
Fruit and pasture appear in the same sequence; this ayah contributes the cultivated and grazed yield of the land.
That produce is provision for people and livestock (مَتَاعًا لَكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ), completing the rain, soil, and crop relation that the section places under divine provision.
The verse asks what people sow (مَا تَحْرُثُونَ), directly naming the plowed field that the section uses to figure what grows from the soul.
It asks whether people or God make the seed grow; this makes the field's fruitfulness in the section an outcome of divine measure, not self-sufficiency.
God could make the crop dry fragments (حُطَامًا); the possible harvest turned barren directly mirrors the section's growing field and cut or buried field.
The one who spreads corruption on earth destroys crops and livestock (وَيُهْلِكَ الْحَرْثَ وَالنَّسْلَ); this is a close reversal of fruitful ground and animal provision under a transgressor.
God created and proportioned (خَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ); this repeats the section's sawwā for formed creation before it turns to what grows and withers.
God measures and guides (قَدَّرَ فَهَدَىٰ); in this sequence it contributes the measured order that precedes pasture and its fate.
God brings out pasture (أَخْرَجَ الْمَرْعَىٰ), the living field side of the section's ground and crop image.
The pasture becomes dark stubble (غُثَاءً أَحْوَىٰ); this gives a precise grown-then-spent counterpart to the section's field made barren.
The verse says the one who purifies himself succeeds (قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَنْ تَزَكَّىٰ), closely restating the purifying path and outcome of the section.
Humanity is shown the path and may be grateful or ungrateful (إِمَّا شَاكِرًا وَإِمَّا كَفُورًا); this directly articulates the two moral possibilities that the section gives the soul.
God guides the human being to the two paths (وَهَدَيْنَاهُ النَّجْدَيْنِ), a direct formulation of choosing between the two courses in the section.
The one who transgresses (طَغَىٰ) is set against the one who restrains himself in the next passage; this same limit-crossing marks Thamud's wrong course in the section.
The one who fears standing before his Lord and restrains the soul from desire (وَنَهَى النَّفْسَ عَنِ الْهَوَىٰ) enacts taqwa as a bridle, directly opposite the soul's unleashed fujūr.
The garden is the refuge of the restrained person; this next ayah completes the preceding inward restraint with its opposite outcome to transgression.
God creates, fashions, and proportions the human being (خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّاكَ فَعَدَلَكَ); the same sawwā root links a formed creature with the section's fashioned sky and leveled settlement.
The righteous are in bliss (إِنَّ الْأَبْرَارَ لَفِي نَعِيمٍ); this gives the good side of the moral division whose next ayah names the wicked.
The wicked (الْفُجَّارَ) are in Hell, using the section's fujūr word for the contrary moral course and its consequence.
Human endeavors are diverse (إِنَّ سَعْيَكُمْ لَشَتَّىٰ); this bridges the paired night and day to the two diverging courses of the section.
The giving person who fears God (أَعْطَىٰ وَاتَّقَىٰ) follows the section's God-conscious and successful path.
Affirming the best completes the description of the good course begun in the prior ayah, before its promised ease.
God promises to ease the God-conscious giver toward ease (فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ), closely matching the section's promise attached to its successful path.
The withholding, self-sufficient person begins the opposite course; this contributes the section's buried and unsuccessful field.
Denial of the best completes the rejecting course described in the preceding ayah, matching the section's denial of the messenger.
The opposite person is eased toward hardship (فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ); it gives a paired contrary outcome to the section's successful course.
Only the most wretched (الْأَشْقَى) enters the fire; the same distinctive word links the self-starting worst man in the section to the consequence of that course.
This person denied the truth and turned away (كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ), which parallels Thamud's denial of their messenger and their refusal of the sign.
The most God-conscious (الْأَتْقَى) is kept away from that fire, setting the section's protected, restrained path against the most wretched one.
The person gives wealth to purify himself (يُؤْتِي مَالَهُ يَتَزَكَّىٰ), supplying another concrete Qur'anic formulation of the section's purifying course.

The girl buried alive (الْمَوْءُودَةُ) is the opposite agent and victim from the soul that buries itself in the section; the parallel makes moral burial a question of responsibility, not just concealment.
The next ayah asks for what sin she was killed (بِأَيِّ ذَنْبٍ قُتِلَتْ); it completes that reversal by exposing the buried victim's innocence rather than blaming her.
After the upheaval of sky and earth, every soul knows what it has brought (عَلِمَتْ نَفْسٌ مَا أَحْضَرَتْ); this makes the section's final, irreversible reckoning of the soul explicit.
Each people is seized for its sin (بِذَنْبِهِ); the different fates include storm, cry, earth-swallowing, and drowning, making the section's sin-and-measured-consequence relation concrete.
The record omits neither small nor great deed (لَا يُغَادِرُ صَغِيرَةً وَلَا كَبِيرَةً); this gives the section's image of each transgressor receiving a measured share the form of a complete account.
Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it; this is the good portion in the section's paired moral outcomes.
Whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it; the next ayah completes the exact balancing of outcome that the section associates with the camel's allotted share and the people's consequence.
Punishment covers people from above and beneath their feet (يَغْشَاهُمُ الْعَذَابُ); this makes the section's judgment closing over Thamud like night explicit.
The angels greet the steadfast with a good final outcome (فَنِعْمَ عُقْبَى الدَّارِ); this uses the section's ʿuqbā word-family for an outcome that contrasts with Thamud's irreversible end.

The phrase “turn back on your heels” (انْقَلَبْتُمْ عَلَىٰ أَعْقَابِكُمْ) uses the literal heel-branch related to the section's ʿuqbā, but here it means apostasy rather than a later consequence; it makes the bodily-root association a deliberate change of sense.
The dry earth stirs and swells after rain; it offers a specific barren-to-living ground parallel to the section's field, though the verse uses it as a resurrection sign.
The earth is humbled and then stirs after rain; this repeats the dry-to-fruitful land boundary in the section, here as a sign of resurrection.
The verse names palms whose fruit is heavy (طَلْعُهَا هَضِيمٌ); that fruitful palm is a specific reversal of the section's secondary reading of ʿaqr as cutting a palm's head so it will not bear.
A destroyed people's roof falls in upon them (فَخَرَّ عَلَيْهِمُ السَّقْفُ); this parallels the section's palaces leveled with their inhabitants, though it speaks of another town.
The verse describes a town collapsed on its roofs and lofty palaces abandoned; that is a close physical parallel to Thamud's flattened settlement, though the people are unnamed here.
Thamud are recalled as cutting into rock in a valley (بِالْوَادِ), adding another account of their built landscape to the section's plain and palaces.
The same Thamud passage says they skillfully hew houses from mountains (تَنْحِتُونَ مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا); this complements the section's palaces on the plain with their mountain dwellings.
This next verse says Satan strips the two people's garment (يَنْزِعُ عَنْهُمَا لِبَاسَهُمَا); beside the garment of taqwa in 7:26, it gives a specific image of a protective covering being torn away.
The one who purifies himself does so for his own soul (وَمَنْ تَزَكَّىٰ فَإِنَّمَا يَتَزَكَّىٰ لِنَفْسِهِ); this repeats the section's purification root, though in a statement about personal benefit.
Charity is said to purify and cleanse (تُطَهِّرُهُمْ وَتُزَكِّيهِمْ بِهَا); it offers a concrete act of tazkiya related to the section's purifying path, though the section does not name charity.
